content: Palmoplantar pustulosis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the presence of sterile, recurrent pustules on the palms and soles. It may also present with additional symptoms. The most recent Cochrane Review on this condition was published in 2006, prior to the widespread use of biological therapies. The objective of this updated review was to evaluate the efficacy of various interventions in achieving and maintaining complete remission of the disease. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed treatments for palmoplantar pustulosis or chronic palmoplantar pustular psoriasis. These treatments included topical therapies, systemic therapies, combinations of topical and systemic therapies, and non-pharmacological interventions. Comparators included placebo, no intervention, or other treatments. The primary outcomes measured were the proportion of participants achieving clearance or near-clearance, the proportion experiencing adverse effects severe enough to cause withdrawal, the proportion with at least a 50% improvement in disease severity, and the proportion with adverse effects. A total of 37 studies involving 1663 participants (mean age 50 years, range 34 to 63; 24% male) were included. The severity of the condition was reported inconsistently across studies. Approximately half of the trials specified their settings, which included hospitals, community clinics, or both. More than half of the studies were at high risk of bias in at least one domain. The majority of the included studies evaluated systemic treatments, such as retinoids, ciclosporin, biologics, etretinate combined with PUVA (psoralens and long-wave ultraviolet radiation), and antibiotics. Other interventions included topical treatments (e.g., corticosteroids, vitamin D derivatives) and phototherapy (e.g., PUVA, ultraviolet A1). Most studies compared these interventions to placebo, and the results were assessed over a short-term period (mean treatment duration of 11 weeks, ranging from 8 to 24 weeks). One trial involving 188 participants compared the topical vitamin D derivative maxacalcitol to placebo. The results suggested that maxacalcitol may be more effective than placebo in achieving clearance (risk ratio [RR] 7.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.85 to 33.12; low-quality evidence). The risk of adverse effects, such as mild local irritation, pruritus, and abnormalities in hematological or urinary tests, was likely similar between the two groups (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.19; moderate-quality evidence). Disease severity was not reported in this trial. Two trials involving 49 participants assessed PUVA therapy compared to placebo or no treatment. The evidence was of very low quality. Adverse effects associated with oral PUVA included nausea, ankle swelling, and non-purulent conjunctivitis, while local PUVA was associated with blistering, erythema, and pruritus. One trial involving 33 participants evaluated the systemic retinoid alitretinoin. The results indicated that alitretinoin likely has little or no effect on reducing disease severity compared to placebo (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.30; moderate-quality evidence). Adverse events, such as headache, cheilitis, nausea, arthralgia, and nasopharyngitis, were reported at similar rates in both groups (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.17). Clearance was not reported in this trial. Regarding biological therapies, one study involving 15 participants suggested that etanercept may have little or no effect on achieving clearance compared to placebo (RR 1.64, 95% CI 0.08 to 34.28; low-quality evidence). However, the wide confidence interval indicates uncertainty, and severity was not measured. Another study involving 33 participants suggested that more patients treated with placebo may achieve reduced severity compared to those treated with ustekinumab, but the wide confidence interval (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.11 to 2.13; low-quality evidence) indicates uncertainty, and clearance was not reported. Two studies involving 154 participants assessed guselkumab. The evidence was of very low quality regarding its effect on clearance. However, guselkumab likely reduces disease severity better than placebo (RR 2.88, 95% CI 1.24 to 6.69; moderate-quality evidence). Secukinumab was also found to likely be superior to placebo in reducing disease severity (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.35; moderate-quality evidence), but clearance was not reported. Adverse effects not requiring withdrawal were not reported for these treatments. Only two of the studies reported adverse effects severe enough to cause withdrawal. Guselkumab may cause more serious adverse events compared to placebo, but the evidence is uncertain due to a very wide confidence interval (RR 2.88, 95% CI 0.32 to 25.80; low-quality evidence). Secukinumab likely causes more serious adverse events than placebo (RR 3.29, 95% CI 1.40 to 7.75; moderate-quality evidence). In conclusion, there is a lack of robust evidence for commonly used treatments for chronic palmoplantar pustulosis, such as superpotent corticosteroids, phototherapy, acitretin, methotrexate, and ciclosporin. The evidence is limited by risk of bias and imprecision. Maxacalcitol may be more effective than placebo in achieving clearance in the short term, with a similar risk of adverse effects. Oral alitretinoin likely has no significant effect on reducing severity, with a comparable risk of adverse effects. The effects of etanercept on clearance and ustekinumab on severity remain uncertain. Secukinumab and guselkumab are likely more effective than placebo in reducing severity, but adverse events not requiring withdrawal were not consistently reported. Future trials should focus on commonly used treatments and employ validated measures of disease severity and quality of life.
